book_title: From neuron shape to noisy spike trains
purpose: Exact enrichment figure set requested for textbook-style infrastructure.

figures.caption: Different neuron shapes, same signaling job. Real neurons differ greatly in shape, but all still have receiving regions, a trigger zone, and an output path.
figures.alt_text: Gallery of several neuron morphologies showing diverse branching patterns and cell-body positions.
figures.source_anchor: OpenStax morphology framing and Allen/real cell resources
figures.is_not: A complete functional classification of neuron types.

figures.caption: A simplified signaling map of a neuron. The cartoon removes detail so the reader can track where input arrives, where spikes begin, and where output goes.
figures.alt_text: Simplified neuron with labeled dendrites, soma, axon hillock, axon, and terminals.
figures.is_not: A portrait of every real neuron.

figures.caption: Different ions are unevenly distributed across the membrane. The pattern, not the exact number, is the key beginner lesson.
figures.alt_text: Bar chart comparing intracellular and extracellular concentrations of four major ions.
figures.source_anchor: OpenStax membrane section and current minibook emphasis
figures.is_not: A universal measurement for every neuron.

figures.caption: Electrochemical force combines two pushes. Diffusion and electrical attraction can oppose each other, and the balance point defines a reversal potential.
figures.alt_text: Diagram showing potassium pushed outward by concentration and inward by negative interior.

figures.caption: Membrane potential is a voltage difference. A neuron's inside is measured relative to the outside reference.
figures.alt_text: Cell membrane with recording electrode inside and reference outside, meter reading negative voltage.
figures.is_not: A statement that the whole cell interior is strongly negative.

figures.caption: Synapses change postsynaptic voltage. The same neuron may be pushed toward or away from threshold depending on which channels open.
figures.alt_text: Presynaptic terminal releasing transmitter onto postsynaptic membrane, with excitatory and inhibitory examples.

figures.caption: Small inputs can combine before a spike begins. Threshold depends on the total membrane effect of multiple graded inputs.
figures.alt_text: Graph of multiple graded potentials summing toward a threshold line.

figures.caption: The action potential is a stereotyped voltage event. Fast sodium entry drives the rise; delayed potassium effects help end the spike and reset the membrane.
figures.alt_text: Voltage trace with labeled phases and threshold line.
figures.is_not: A raw recording from a specific cell.

figures.caption: Storyboard for an action potential animation. Each frame should pair channel state with the matching segment of the voltage trace.
figures.alt_text: Text storyboard describing successive phases of an action potential animation.
figures.source_anchor: Action potential and channel timing concepts

figures.caption: A stronger message is often more spikes, not taller spikes. Information can be carried by firing rate and timing, not by action-potential amplitude.
figures.alt_text: Raster plots and rate annotations showing more frequent spikes in stronger conditions.
figures.source_anchor: Current minibook and action-potential all-or-none framing
figures.is_not: A complete theory of neural coding.

figures.caption: Hodgkin-Huxley turns membrane biophysics into a circuit language. The membrane stores charge, while ion-channel pathways pull voltage toward their reversal potentials.
figures.alt_text: Membrane represented by capacitor with sodium, potassium, and leak branches.
figures.source_anchor: HH circuit interpretation and NEURON/NetPyNE relevance
figures.is_not: Literal metal electronics inside a neuron.

figures.caption: Single channels open all-or-none, but at variable times. Patch clamp made channel randomness experimentally visible.
figures.alt_text: Pipette attached to membrane and a current trace jumping between closed and open states.
figures.source_anchor: Patch clamp significance and Nobel-linked impact

figures.caption: Small fluctuations can shift threshold crossing time. Near threshold, noise changes spike timing even when the average input is similar.
figures.alt_text: Voltage traces and spike-timing summaries comparing low-, medium-, and high-noise conditions.
figures.source_anchor: Allen/ModelDB/NEURON-compatible modeling workflow and current minibook project arc
figures.is_not: A real Allen or DANDI recording.
